planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; the compact bird's-nest rosette suits a small pot or dish garden.

directions: This Hahnii-group hybrid was bred by crossing the tall, white-edged Laurentii with the dwarf, nest-forming Hahnii, producing a low, flattened rosette of broad gray-green leaves with faint cross-banding and a slim pale margin. It keeps the compact, stemless habit of its Hahnii parent while showing softer, more silvery leaf color than plain Hahnii or its golden-edged sport. Give it bright indirect light to keep the coloring crisp, and let the gritty succulent mix dry out fully between waterings since the thick leaves rot quickly if kept wet. New rosettes form at the base as it matures and can be separated with a bit of root attached to start new pots.

planting.note: Pot singly or in small clusters in a very gritty succulent mix with a tall, narrow container to support the upright cylindrical leaves; grow in bright indirect light.

directions: Native to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, this species grows as one or two stiff, pencil-thin, cylindrical leaves rising straight up from the base rather than a fan of flat blades, with faint light-green horizontal streaking and a dark furrow running down one side. Fresh growth emerges wrapped in a short purplish sheath that dries and papers over as the leaf matures, a feature this species shows more strongly than most of its flat-leaved relatives. Because each stem stands alone rather than clustering densely, a potted grouping of several leaves of different ages gives the most striking display. Keep it in bright light and let the mix dry completely between waterings, since the rod-like leaves store enough water to tolerate long dry spells but rot readily in soggy soil.

planting.note: Grow in a shallow, wide pot with gritty succulent mix and bright indirect light to keep the thick, blue-gray leaves compact and richly colored.

directions: This selection of the East African species kirkii is grown for its stiff, channeled leaves in a cool blue-gray tone overlaid with darker mottled blotches and a thin wavy reddish edge, a color combination distinct from the plain green species or the coppery-bronze 'Coppertone' selection. It stays low and flat, spreading slowly into a wide rosette rather than growing tall, so it suits a shallow bowl or dish garden better than a deep pot. Give it bright indirect light to intensify the blue cast of the leaves, since deep shade tends to flatten the color toward plain green. Water only when the gritty mix is bone dry, and divide rooted offsets from the base to start new plants.

planting.note: Grow in a deep pot with fast-draining succulent mix and bright indirect light; this upright species needs more room than dwarf snake plant types.

directions: Native to West and Central Africa, this species forms an upright, stemless rosette of broad, glossy, grayish-green leaves marked with irregular light horizontal striping, scaling up to a noticeably larger and more substantial plant than the common trifasciata houseplant forms. Its wide leaf blades and clumping habit give it a bolder, more architectural presence in a container than slender-leaved snake plants, making it a good floor specimen once mature. It shares the genus's tolerance for neglect, storing water in thick leaves and needing only infrequent watering once the gritty mix has dried completely. Propagate by dividing offsets from the base of an established clump rather than relying on slow leaf cuttings.
